questions.prompt: Which ACID property guarantees that a transaction's effects survive a subsequent system crash?
questions.explanation: Durability means committed changes persist, normally ensured by forcing log records to stable storage before acknowledging the commit. Atomicity is all-or-nothing, not persistence.

questions.prompt: A schedule is conflict serializable if and only if:

options.text: All reads occur before all writes

questions.explanation: Build a node per transaction and an edge Ti → Tj for each conflicting pair where Ti acts first. The schedule is conflict serializable exactly when this graph has no cycle.

questions.prompt: Two operations conflict if they belong to different transactions, access the same data item, and:

options.text: At least one of them is a write
They occur in the same transaction

questions.explanation: Read–read pairs commute and do not conflict. Read–write, write–read and write–write pairs do, because swapping them can change the outcome.

questions.prompt: Which isolation level permits non-repeatable reads but prevents dirty reads?
questions.explanation: READ COMMITTED only ever reads committed data, so no dirty reads, but it does not hold read locks to completion — so re-reading a row may yield a different value.

questions.prompt: A 'dirty read' occurs when a transaction:

options.text: Reads the same row twice and gets different values
Reads a row that was deleted before it started
Reads a value written by another transaction that has not yet committed
Writes over another transaction's uncommitted write

questions.explanation: Reading uncommitted data is dangerous because the writer may abort, leaving the reader having acted on a value that never existed — a cascading rollback.

questions.prompt: A schedule is said to be cascadeless (avoids cascading rollback) if:

options.text: The precedence graph is a tree
All writes happen at commit time
Every transaction reads only values written by committed transactions

questions.explanation: If a transaction never reads uncommitted data, one abort can never force others to roll back. Every cascadeless schedule is recoverable, but not vice versa.

questions.prompt: Consider the schedule: r1(X), w1(X), r2(X), w2(X), r1(Y), w1(Y), commit1, commit2. Is it conflict serializable?

options.text: Yes — equivalent to T1 followed by T2
No — the precedence graph has a cycle
Yes — equivalent to T2 followed by T1
It cannot be determined without knowing the values

questions.explanation: The only conflicts are on X, and every T1 operation on X precedes every T2 operation, giving the single edge T1 → T2. Y is touched by T1 alone, so the graph is acyclic and the serial order is T1, T2.

questions.prompt: Which anomaly does the SERIALIZABLE isolation level prevent that REPEATABLE READ (in the classic ANSI definition) does not?
questions.explanation: A phantom appears when a re-executed range query returns newly inserted rows. Preventing it needs predicate or index-range locking, which is what SERIALIZABLE adds over REPEATABLE READ.

questions.prompt: In the transaction state diagram, a transaction moves from 'partially committed' to 'committed' when:

options.text: Its log records have been written to stable storage

questions.explanation: Executing the last statement only reaches 'partially committed'. The transaction is truly committed once enough log information is on stable storage to guarantee its effects survive a crash.

questions.prompt: Every conflict-serializable schedule is also view serializable. Which statement completes the relationship correctly?

options.text: Every view-serializable schedule is conflict serializable
View serializability is a stricter condition
Some view-serializable schedules are not conflict serializable — these contain blind writes

questions.explanation: Conflict serializability is a strict subset of view serializability. The schedules in the gap always involve blind writes — a write with no preceding read of that item by the same transaction.
